title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

title: Genomic insights into activated antimicrobial resistance of in situ hospital-wastewater biofilm

Remote realities: In-depth conversations on antimicrobial stewardship in remote Indigenous communities using a One Health approach
Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

title: Virulence attenuation in ST11-K64 Klebsiella pneumoniae explains its divergent clinical manifestation from ST23-K1

Genetic determinants of hypervirulence with attenuated pathogenicity in a bla(NDM-1)-encoding Klebsiella pneumoniae causing neonatal sepsis
Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Bridging soil resistome and clinical inference: A four-tier evidentiary framework
Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

Influence of Gliricidia sepium living support on rhizosphere bacterial recruitment and fruit metabolomics in black pepper (Piper nigrum)
abstract: The ability of the rhizosphere to recruit beneficial microorganisms is central to the sustainable management of crops. Here, we investigated, through shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mass spectrometry techniques, the microbial composition, antimicrobial resistance (AMRs), and metabolomic profiles of Piper nigrum cultivated under two support systems: living Gliricidia sepium support (SL/RL) and dead wooden support (SD/RD). Bulk and rhizosphere soils were sequenced to assess taxonomic structure and ARGs, with emphasis on Actinobacteria due to their relevance in antibiotic production. Actinobacteria were highly represented across the samples (~ 35%). Dead-support rhizospheres exhibited a broader ARG repertoire and greater abundance of taxa known to include antibiotic-producing members, whereas living-support rhizospheres showed reduced ARG diversity. Metabolomic analysis further revealed support-dependent physiological responses in the host plant. PLS-DA distinguished the two cultivation systems, and three defense-related flavonoids, such as sakuranetin, isovitexin, and orientin, which were enriched in fruits of plants grown with dead support, indicating activation of stress - and defense - associated metabolic pathways. Their low abundance in living-support plants suggests reduced physiological stress, likely linked to improved nutrient cycling and rhizosphere stability provided by G. sepium. However, the volatile and total phenolic profile did not display significant chemical alterations in the samples. Together, these results suggest that support type influences both microbial functions and plant secondary metabolism. Dead support creates a more stressful ecological context that enriches antimicrobial resistance genes ARGs and defense metabolites, whereas living support promotes a more balanced soil-plant-microbe environment, supporting the use of G. sepium as a sustainable and biologically advantageous cultivation strategy for black pepper.

title: Rv0783c of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Acts as a Proton-Motive Force Dependent Multidrug Efflux Transporter Involved in the Efflux of Structurally Unrelated Antibiotics and Enhancing Biofilm Formation
abstract: Despite multiple treatment strategies and extensive research on resistance mechanisms, tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health concern, largely because of the rise of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. Among various mechanisms complicating the situation, active antibiotic export via efflux pumps is particularly significant, yet largely unexplored. Mycobacterium sp. encodes numerous transporters, many of which are overexpressed in clinical isolates or under drug stress. Here, we examined the possible role of Rv0783c, a putative transporter that is reportedly overexpressed in drug-stressed conditions. Rv0783c conferred resistance to multiple structurally diverse antibiotics, fluoroquinolones and anti-TB drugs in the heterologous hosts, namely, Escherichia coli and Mycobacterium smegmatis. Reduced drug accumulation and active efflux of ethidium bromide (EtBr) confirmed its transport activity, which in turn gets nullified upon using the proton-motive force blocker, CCCP (Carbonyl Cyanide m-Chlorophenylhydrazone). On the other hand, its expression enhanced biofilm formation, linking antibiotic resistance to persistence-associated phenotype. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis confirmed the presence of crucial interacting residues with antibiotics that were identified by in silico analysis. Overall, we demonstrate the role of Rv0783c in the extrusion of first and second-line anti-TB drugs and enhancing biofilm formation.

title: Author Correction: Global genomic surveillance uncovers emergence and spatiotemporal patterns of World Health Organization priority antibiotic resistance in invasive Salmonella
Antibiotic resistance of bacteria isolated from microbiological control of gastrointestinal endoscopes
abstract: Numerous infections and outbreaks linked to insufficient disinfection of thermosensitive endoscopes have been reported in recent years. The effectiveness of endoscope reprocessing is typically monitored via microbiological controls that detect indicator microorganisms. Resistance profile is rarely assessed in routine surveillance of indicator isolates. To evaluate antibiotic resistance among indicator bacteria isolated from routine surveillance samples of gastrointestinal endoscopes and to determine risk factors for endoscopes' contamination. Antibiograms were performed on all indicator bacteria recovered from control samples of digestive endoscopes at Brest university hospital between 2016 and 2024. A multivariable regression model was done to identify risk factor for contamination. During the study period, 99 distinct indicator bacteria were recovered from 65 endoscope controls. Overall, 15.2% of isolates exhibited acquired antibiotic resistance. Among 41 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, 3 were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins, 6 to carbapenems, and 5 to quinolones. Of 54 Enterobacterales isolates, 17 resisted third-generation cephalosporins (including 6 ESBL producers), 12 were resistant to aminoglycosides, and 12 to quinolones. No carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales were identified. One of three Enterococcus spp. isolates was resistant to amoxicillin. Risk for endoscopes' contamination significantly increased with age of device. This study is the first to evaluate resistance profiles of indicator bacteria isolated from gastrointestinal endoscopes during regular microbiological surveillance. It highlights the potential role of inadequate disinfection in the cross-transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacteria during endoscopic procedures.

title: Epidemiology of multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and performance of molecular genotypic drug susceptibility testing in Papua New Guinea, 2022-2023
abstract: Papua New Guinea (PNG) is a high burden country for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Contemporary data is needed given the introduction of a new MDR-TB treatment regimen. We aimed to describe the epidemiology of MDR-TB from 2022 to 2023 and evaluate the performance of the Xpert MTB/XDR assay in PNG. Molecular testing was conducted at district/provincial laboratories and the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL), and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) at the Queensland Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory. We included cases with Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and MTB/XDR results to describe the epidemiology of MDR-TB. Specimens with Xpert MTB/XDR and phenotypic DST results were used to evaluate the performance of molecular testing modalities compared to phenotypic DST. 206 MDR-TB and 20 pre-XDR-TB diagnostic cases were included, predominantly from Western Province (111, 49%; 18.5 referred cases/100,000 population/year) and National Capital District (86, 38%; 5.7 referred cases/100,000 population/year). The most common risk factor was MDR-TB exposure (67/226, 30%). The Xpert MTB/XDR assay showed high sensitivity and specificity for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance. PNG continues to have a remarkably high incidence of MDR-TB. Risk factor data highlights the importance of contact management. Despite challenges, molecular diagnostics perform well and can improve MDR-TB detection.

title: Dual therapy is associated with synchronous gonococcal susceptible-zone MIC dynamics: Norway, 2013-2025
abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has repeatedly overcome every antibiotic class deployed against it. Antimicrobial resistance surveillance systems that focus on resistance prevalence may contribute to delayed realisation that a bacterial population is adapting to empiric treatment regimes. As new antibiotics zoliflodacin and gepotidacin will soon be launched in Norway, this study aimed to explore how surveillance might detect subtle gonococcal minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) shifts, by focusing on the susceptible-zone, using the dual therapy era as a 'natural experiment'. We also aimed to map the population antibiotic co-resistance landscapes that will confront the new antimicrobial agents. In this retrospective, population-based, descriptive study, the recently introduced 'susceptible isolate pressure indicator' ratio (SIPI) was applied to 13 years of per-isolate Norwegian gonococcal surveillance data (2013-2025; n = 8,230 isolates) to characterise susceptible-zone MIC dynamics during and after the dual therapy era. Annual Kendall τ-b correlations between full MIC distributions of the dual therapy agents and legacy antibiotics were plotted to characterise the evolving cross-resistance landscape. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin SIPI trajectories moved in close synchrony throughout the dual-therapy period and diverged after the 2020 treatment policy change. Divergence timing differed by anatomical site. Male anal and pharyngeal isolates followed distinct trajectories. Post-dual therapy, ceftriaxone and azithromycin SIPI trends were consistent with model predictions for changing selective pressure. Susceptible-zone MIC distributions may contain resistance emergence information not captured by conventional surveillance metrics. The SIPI ratio may offer an innovative framework for monitoring future treatment policy decisions.

title: Occurrence of macrolide antibiotics in drinking water sources and their potential health risks
abstract: Macrolide antibiotics (MLAs) are widely utilized in both human and veterinary medicine. Their extensive use has led to ubiquitous contamination in aquatic environments, posing significant risks to public health and ecosystems. Despite their prevalence, comprehensive analyses of their environmental fate, diverse exposure pathways, and potential molecular toxicological mechanisms remain insufficient. This study systematically reviewed MLAs in global drinking water sources from 2005 to 2025 and their potential impacts on health. Using VOSviewer for bibliometric analysis, key research clusters focusing on ecological risks, antimicrobial resistance development, and health outcomes were identified. MLAs are frequently detected in surface and groundwater, with concentrations exceeding 1000 ng/L in specific regions, primarily influenced by seasonal variations and regional industrial activities. Additionally, we assessed how MLAs through the food chain into human dietary sources such as seafood and dairy products. Clinically, MLAs exposure correlates with a range of adverse health outcomes including cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation), hearing loss, obesity, and developmental defects. Five representative toxicity pathways were reviewed: mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy/apoptosis, hERG potassium channel blockade, altered bile acid homeostasis, nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) inhibition, and oxidative stress. The evidence supporting these pathways varies across individual macrolides, and their relevance to exposure through drinking water remains uncertain. By identifying existing research gaps, this review establishes a robust scientific foundation for risk assessment and calls for enhanced oversight to mitigate the environmental and health risks associated with MLAs.

title: Longitudinal evaluation of a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control bundle in a high AMR prevalence ICU
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a major threat in intensive care units (ICUs). We evaluated changes associated with a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control (IPC) bundle in a high-AMR-prevalence setting. This longitudinal quasi-experimental ICU study (2022-2024) involved sequential, cumulative implementation of a bundle integrating infection prevention, rapid diagnostics and colonization screening, antimicrobial stewardship, and surveillance with data feedback. Hand hygiene compliance increased from 29.5% at baseline to 64.6% during sustainment, while PPE compliance increased from 67.1% to 73.3% after monitoring was introduced. Piperacillin/tazobactam consumption increased (+3.33 DDD/100 patient-days per phase; 95% CI, 1.92-4.73), whereas colistin (-5.85; 95% CI, -9.17 to -2.54) and tigecycline (-2.50; 95% CI, -4.25 to -0.75) decreased. Klebsiella pneumoniae meropenem resistance decreased (OR per phase, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.43-0.69), whereas colistin resistance showed a borderline increase in Acinetobacter baumannii (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.00-1.65). ICU-acquired bloodstream infections decreased across implementation phases for CRE (IRR per phase, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.26-0.51) and CRAB (IRR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.46-0.68), as did CLABSI (IRR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.56-0.73) and ICU-acquired rectal colonization with CRE (IRR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.63-0.84) and CRAB (IRR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.70-0.87), whereas CRPA ICU-acquired colonization increased (IRR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.32-1.85). IPC bundle implementation was followed by improved IPC practices and reductions in several ICU-acquired infections and colonization outcomes; continued surveillance and stewardship are essential.

title: Plasmid-plasmid interactions reshape extracellular vesicle cargo and antimicrobial resistance gene transfer potential
abstract: Plasmids are major drivers of bacterial horizontal gene transfer, including transfer of antimicrobial resistance. Plasmid dissemination extends beyond conjugation to include extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated transport. Although bacterial EVs can carry plasmid DNA, mechanisms governing which plasmids are incorporated into EVs remain poorly understood. Here, we tested whether principles of conjugative plasmid transfer, including effects of plasmid mobility type and plasmid-plasmid interactions, extend to EV-mediated export. Using model conjugative (pKJK5) and mobilizable (RSF1010) resistance plasmids in two independent hosts, we quantified plasmid incorporation into EVs under single- and dual-plasmid conditions. Despite its lower intracellular copy number, the conjugative pKJK5 was preferentially incorporated into EVs, exceeding RSF1010 by 10- to 23-fold under single-plasmid carriage. Under co-residence, this pattern reversed: RSF1010 enrichment increased by 13- to 39-fold, whereas pKJK5 incorporation decreased by 2- to 7-fold, strongly deviating from stochastic expectations based on intracellular abundance, with effects conserved across hosts. This indicates that mobilizable plasmids exploit conjugative transfer machinery to access membrane-associated sites of preferential EV formation, thereby increasing their likelihood of EV incorporation. This demonstrates that EV cargo composition is not stochastic but is actively reshaped by plasmid-specific properties and plasmid-plasmid interactions, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism influencing gene transfer in microbial communities.

title: A dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle delivery system for precision phage therapy against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria
abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among Gram-negative bacteria, demands innovative therapeutic strategies. Here, we present a dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle-chimeric phage (AbLCP) system engineered to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria. Our design integrates a genetically modified M13 phage displaying anti-lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antibodies with polymyxin B conjugation, which is further encapsulated within anti-LPS antibody-functionalized lipid nanoparticles. This system overcomes the fundamental limitations of conventional phage therapy, enabling efficient cellular internalization, endosomal escape, and potent intracellular bactericidal activity. In murine models ofinfection, AbLCP achieved superior bacterial clearance and up to 10-fold reduction in bacterial burden at a 10-fold lower effective dose than free polymyxin B, with 67-fold selective accumulation at infection sites, and attenuated systemic inflammation and preservation of gut microbiota. Mechanistically, AbLCP neutralized LPS to suppress inflammation and induced a lethal bacterial stress response. This work establishes a transformative nanophage platform that merges synthetic biology with nanomedicine, offering a promising strategy against MDR bacterial infections.

title: Molecular Glue Degraders of TEM β-Lactamases by Periplasmic Protease DegP
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the most serious challenges to global health, yet the development of new molecules with novel mechanisms of action to combat resistance is lacking. In this study, we report the discovery of molecular glues that recruit TEM-family β-lactamases to the bacterial protease DegP for degradation. β-Lactamase inhibitor tazobactam was found to accelerate degradation of TEM β-lactamases by DegP, which was further enhanced by linkerless incorporation of dipeptide motifs enriched among DegP substrates. The resulting molecular glue degraders showed improved synergy with β-lactam piperacillin against resistant Escherichia coli compared to tazobactam, as well as good pharmacokinetic properties for oral dosing. Collectively, this work establishes periplasmic targeted protein degradation as a promising new mechanism for combating β-lactamase resistance.

title: Occurrence of carbapenemase genes and phenotypic colistin resistance in wastewater from Kütahya, Türkiye
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global threat that requires coordinated, international action. Recent work highlights how AMR in surface waters affects ecosystems, agriculture, and human health within a One Health framework. The spread of resistance is driven by widespread antibiotic use, self-medication, and inadequate treatment. This study evaluated microbial density and the prevalence of carbapenemase and colistin resistance genes in wastewater treatment plants in Kütahya, Turkey, incorporating seasonal variation. Using conventional and molecular microbiology approaches qualitative and targeted qPCR analysis a total of 60 wastewater samples were screened for key resistance determinants. Multiple carbapenemase genes were detected, including bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, and bla, with blaand blabeing the most frequent. Numerical differences in resistance-gene detection frequencies were observed between the two sampling periods; however, these differences were not statistically significant. bla, bla, and blapredominated in summer, whereas bla, bla, and blawere more common in winter. Mobilized colistin resistance genes (mcr) mcr-1 to mcr-5 were not detected in any of the 60 wastewater samples under the assay conditions used, while the number of detected resistance genes per sample ranged from zero to seven. Overall, the results indicate that wastewater treatment systems may represent important environmental reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance determinants, raising concerns regarding their potential dissemination into receiving environments and underscoring the need for continued surveillance and effective wastewater management.

title: Emergence of vancomycin-resistant and multidrug-resistant Enterococcus spp. in freshwater aquaculture systems of southeastern Nigeria: implications for one health surveillance
abstract: Freshwater aquaculture is increasingly recognised as a reservoir for antimicrobial-resistant bacteria with consequences for human, animal, and ecosystem health. This study characterised Enterococcus spp. from aquaculture systems in Owerri, southeastern Nigeria. Eighty-three specimens were collected from four fishponds: fish body swabs, pond wall swabs, sediment, and surface water. Enterococci were isolated on selective agar and identified phenotypically; a subset of 60 isolates (50% of the collection) was confirmed by 16 S rRNA gene sequencing. Susceptibility to ten agents was tested by Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion following CLSI guidelines, and the sequenced subset was screened by PCR for resistance determinants. A total of 120 isolates were obtained: E. faecalis (37.5%), E. faecium (25.8%), and unresolved Enterococcus spp. (36.7%). Sequencing confirmed 90% of phenotypic identifications and reassigned 10% as E. hirae, E. casseliflavus, or E. faecium. Resistance was highest against vancomycin (75.8%), quinupristin/dalfopristin (71.7%), erythromycin (65.8%), and ciprofloxacin (65.8%). Among the 100 isolates resistant to at least three agents, all had MAR indices above 0.2, and 31 resisted all ten agents. Multivariable analysis linked surface water recovery (OR 3.24; 95% CI 1.42-7.39) and MAR ≥ 0.6 (OR 4.56; 95% CI 1.89-11.02) with vancomycin resistance. Sixty-two resistance patterns indicated substantial diversity. These findings position Nigerian freshwater aquaculture as a reservoir for clinically relevant resistance, supporting antimicrobial stewardship and One Health surveillance.

title: Virulence and genetic determinants of Staphylococcus spp. in human mastitis: a prevalence study
abstract: Lactational mastitis is a common inflammatory breast disease affecting breastfeeding women and is associated with Staphylococcus spp. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and virulence among these pathogens complicate treatment and emphasize the need for accurate laboratory diagnostic methods. This study investigated the microbiological profile, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence characteristics of Staphylococcus spp. isolated from lactational mastitis and evaluated the correlation between phenotypic and molecular detection of major virulence and methicillin-resistance determinants. A cross-sectional study was conducted in central Gujarat, India, using 180 human milk samples collected from 150 women with lactational mastitis and 30 healthy lactating controls. Somatic cell count, bacterial isolation, biochemical identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, haemolysis, slime production, biofilm assays, polymerase chain reaction detection of the hla, icaA, and mecA genes, and phylogenetic analysis were performed. All mastitis samples exhibited somatic cell counts exceeding 1,000 cells/µL, whereas healthy controls remained below this threshold (p < 0.001). Staphylococcus spp. accounted for 89.4% of isolates. The icaA, hla, and mecA genes were detected in 76.39%, 54.65%, and 46.58% of isolates, respectively. Phenotypically, biofilm formation, alpha-haemolysis, and cefoxitin resistance were observed in 72.67%, 52.79%, and 37.88% of isolates, respectively. Excellent agreement was observed between the corresponding phenotypic and molecular findings, with κ values of 0.89 for icaA/biofilm formation, 0.97 for hla/alpha-haemolysis, and 0.89 for mecA/cefoxitin resistance. Elevated somatic cell count effectively distinguished mastitis from healthy controls. The high prevalence of virulent and antimicrobial-resistant Staphylococcus spp., particularly mecA-positive isolates, underscores the need for continuous surveillance, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and cost-effective phenotypic screening to support routine clinical diagnosis and epidemiological monitoring.

title: Putative conjugative transfer and persistence of carbapenem resistance gene bla(OXA-72) from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRA) has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in clinical settings. In this study, we explored the transfer potential of a mobilizable plasmid-harboringgene betweenspecies originating from patients, municipal wastewater, and pig farm wastewater. PCR-based evidence suggested putative transfer offromto. In this pair, the apparent frequency of PCR-marker-positive putative transconjugants varied depending on temperature and meropenem supplementation, with a higher frequency observed at 27°C than at 17°C and 37°C. Likewise, the presence of antibiotic pressure yielded a higher apparent conjugation frequency; however, this observation was limited to a single donor-recipient pair. Further, we revealed a phenotypic conversion in terms of meropenem susceptibility and a fitness cost in the putative transconjugants. While whole-genome sequencing did not conclusively verify the presence ofor a fully resolved plasmid configuration, Oxford Nanopore read mapping consistently detected the chromosomalgene in all isolates. In contrast, only a limited number of reads aligned with thegene,, or the complete plasmid sequences. Comparative analyses further revealed variations in the composition of surface-associated factors and defense systems of the recipient strains, which could be considered as barriers to conjugation. Lastly, the persistence of PCR-detectable marker genes in putative transconjugants was variable and generally unstable over a 30-day period. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into the factors that may influence horizontal gene transfer and short-term maintenance of.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant(CRA) is a serious clinical concern linked to elevated morbidity and mortality. This study shed light on how the carbapenemase genespreads in the environment via horizontal gene transfer. Using isolates ofandfrom municipal wastewater treatment plants, we show that PCR-based evidence of putative conjugative transfer of thegene depends on temperature and antibiotic exposure. The process also incurs fitness costs, and the transferred gene persists only briefly in recipient cells. These results emphasize the importance of environmental sources as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance gene exchange. Additionally, variations in surface structures and defense systems may act as potential barriers to conjugation. Overall, the work improves our understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) movement and supports the need for better integrated surveillance under a One Health approach.

title: Comparative distribution of antimicrobial resistance genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella from chicken and aquaculture production systems, 2010-2025: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: To compare the prevalence and distribution of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella from chicken and aquaculture production systems and assess regional and temporal patterns of resistance genes, six databases were searched for studies published between 2010 and 2025 reporting AMR genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella. Seventy-six studies met the inclusion criteria, including 68 from chicken and eight from aquaculture. Random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled prevalence. Pooled Salmonella prevalence was 21.0% (95% CI 15.3-28.2) in chicken and 44.3% (95% CI 22.6-68.4) in aquaculture, although aquaculture estimates were based on fewer studies. Resistance genes associated with tetracyclines, β-lactams and sulfonamides were frequently detected, particularly tet(A), blaTEM, blaCTX and sul2. Chicken isolates showed substantial regional heterogeneity, with higher prevalence in the Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia regions. Prevalence of selected genes, including tet(A), sul2, aadA and qnrS, increased across sampling periods. Overlapping AMR gene profiles across chicken and aquaculture suggest interconnected resistance reservoirs that may increase opportunities for human exposure through the food chain, highlighting the importance of integrated AMR surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship strategies.

title: Performance of mCIM/eCIM in Enterobacterales strains co-encoding NDM and OXA-48-like carbapenemases from South India
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRE) are an increasing public health concern, particularly as carbapenemase-producing isolates, such as NDM and OXA-48-like producers, become more prevalent. Rapid and accurate identification of carbapenemases is crucial to guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Although recent epidemiologic data show that CRE increasingly harbor multiple carbapenemases, the performance of common phenotypic tests-the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) and EDTA-modified CIM (eCIM)-has not been well defined in these isolates. We examined the performance of mCIM and eCIM among CRE-encoding NDM, OXA-48-like, or both. We included 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encoding CRE isolates from perirectal swabs collected from patients admitted to two intensive care units at a hospital in South India. Isolates included(53.5%),(41.3%), andspecies (5.3%). Overall, 112 isolates (65.1%) encoded NDM alone, 23 (13.4%) encoded OXA-48-like alone, and 37 (21.5%) encoded both NDM and OXA-48-like. mCIM positivity was 98.2% for NDM, 47.8% for OXA-48-like, and 94.6% for NDM+OXA-48-like encoders; among mCIM-positive isolates, eCIM positivity rates were 99.1%, 91%, and 97.1%, respectively. When compared to molecular carbapenemase gene detection, mCIM/eCIM was highly sensitive for classifying isolates encoding NDM as metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers, but significantly misclassified isolates encoding OXA-48-like as having an MBL or lacking a carbapenemase. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA-48-like co-encoding CRE isolates to date, mCIM/eCIM typically reported these as MBL producers. Carbapenemase-encodinginfections are associated with substantial adverse health outcomes, making rapid and accurate carbapenemase detection essential for guiding antibiotic therapy. Althoughcarrying multiple carbapenemases are increasingly reported worldwide, the performance of common phenotypic assays, mCIM and eCIM, remains insufficiently defined for these strains. In this study of 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encodingisolates from hospitalized patients in South India, mCIM/eCIM consistently classified NDM-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase encoders. Additionally, mCIM/eCIM frequently misclassified OXA-48-like-encoding isolates as either metallo-β-lactamase encoders or carbapenemase-negative, highlighting the need to better understand the mechanisms underlying this variable activity. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA co-encodingisolates reported to date, mCIM/eCIM generally reported co-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase producers. Our results suggest that mCIM/eCIM performance may vary geographically due to variable activity, distribution, and combinations of carbapenemases.

title: Metal-organic frameworks for antibiotic removal from water and wastewater
abstract: The persistence of antibiotics in aquatic environments has emerged as a critical environmental challenge due to their extensive use, incomplete metabolism, and continuous release from municipal, hospital, and industrial sources. Their accumulation in water and wastewater systems fosters antimicrobial resistance, disrupts ecosystems, and poses severe risks to public health. Conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon and zeolites often fall short in terms of selectivity, regeneration, and adsorption capacity, necessitating innovative alternatives. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with their tunable porosity, high surface areas, adjustable chemical functionalities, and structural diversity, have attracted significant attention as next-generation adsorbents for antibiotic removal. This review provides a comprehensive discussion of the occurrence and impacts of antibiotics in aquatic systems, followed by a critical evaluation of the adsorption performance of pristine MOFs, MOF derivatives, and MOF-based composites. Emphasis is placed on synthetic methodologies, purification/activation strategies, and mechanistic insights underlying antibiotic-MOF interactions. Furthermore, the study highlights the regeneration potential of MOFs for sustainable applications, compares their performance with conventional adsorbents, and identifies the persisting challenges in stability, scalability, and selectivity. Finally, knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined, focusing on defect engineering, hybrid frameworks, and other critical factors governing efficient application in real wastewater treatment to accelerate the translation of laboratory studies into practical deployment. By consolidating advances and challenges, this work positions MOFs as promising candidates for addressing the global threat of antibiotic pollution in water and wastewater.

title: Bacterial epidemiology and attributable mortality of Ventilator-associated pneumonia before and after COVID-19 pandemic (2018-2021)
abstract: BackgroundVentilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in mechanically ventilated patients. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly modified VAP epidemiology and microbial ecology.MethodsWe conducted a prospective multicenter cohort study within the REA-REZO network (≈20% of French ICU beds), 1 January 2018-31 December 2021. All adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were included. VAP was defined according to ECDC criteria. Primary endpoints were VAP incidence density (per 1000 ventilation-days) and 30-day attributable mortality. Secondary endpoints included resistance patterns and pre-pandemic versus pandemic trends.ResultsAmong 98,047 patients, 12,251 patients developed VAP, with an incidence of 18.9/1000 ventilation-days. Peak incidence occurred at day 10 (29/1000 ventilation-days). Thirty-day attributable mortality was 4.9% [95% CI 3.7;6.2], rising to 7.2% [6.0;8.5] at 60 days. Gram-negative bacteria accounted for 78.0% of isolates, predominantly(46%) and(20%). Third-generation cephalosporin resistance reached 27% inand 25% in. The COVID-19 patients had a higher VAP rate (19.5% vs 9.7%, p<0.001) and mortality (36.9% vs 31.0%, p<0.001).ConclusionsVAP remains highly prevalent in French ICUs with substantial attributable mortality. The COVID-19 pandemic nearly doubled VAP incidence and worsened resistance profiles. Intensified prevention bundles during the first 10 days of ventilation and reinforced antimicrobial stewardship are critical.

title: Authors reply: European genomic: An untapped opportunity to strengthen the fight against antimicrobial resistance
Microbiology Galaxy Lab: a community-driven gateway for reproducible and FAIR analysis of microbiological data
abstract: The explosion of microbial omics data has outpaced the ability of many researchers to analyse it, with complex tools and limited computational resources creating barriers to discovery. To address this gap, we present the Microbiology Galaxy Lab (MGL): a free, globally accessible, community-supported platform that combines state-of-the-art analytical power with user-friendly accessibility. Supported by the Galaxy and global microbiology communities, this platform integrates over 315 tool suites and 115 curated workflows, enabling comprehensive metabarcoding, (meta)genomic, (meta)transcriptomic, and (meta)proteomic data analysis within a FAIR-aligned environment. It also supports research in the health and infectious disease sectors, as well as in environmental microbiology. The platform's utility is exemplified through various use cases, including antimicrobial resistance tracking, biomarker prediction, microbiome classification, and functional annotation of key microbes. Built on reproducibility and community engagement, it supports the creation, sharing, and updating of best-practice workflows. Over 35 tutorials and learning paths empower scientists, fostering an ecosystem that keeps resources at the forefront of microbiological data analysis. The MGL enables collective analysis, democratising research, thereby accelerating discovery across the global microbiology community ( microbiology.usegalaxy.org , .eu , .org.au , . fr ).

title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

title: Knowledge of antibiotic resistance and prevalence of antibiotic usage among urban residents of Kochi, India: a community-based cross-sectional study
Diffusion-Mediated Quantification of Dose-Dependent Antifungal Drug Tolerance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global health problem, with drug-resistant fungi posing major challenges for the treatment of immunocompromised patients. Antifungal tolerance is a recently discovered phenomenon, distinct from antifungal resistance, whereby pathogenic fungi grow slowly above minimum inhibitory drug concentrations. We combine physics-based spatiotemporal models with microbiology experiments to quantitatively investigate the emergence of tolerance to all three major classes of antifungal drugs used to treat invasive infections in the multidrug-resistant pathogenic yeast Candidozyma auris (formerly Candida auris). Specifically, we combine Fick's second law, solved using a finite difference method to simulate drug diffusion, with experimental data from disk diffusion assays to determine the concentration ranges associated with the emergence of antifungal-tolerant colonies. Tolerant colonies emerged experimentally within distinct drug concentration ranges for itraconazole, amphotericin B, and caspofungin in patient-derived C. auris isolates. This study provides a method to quantify dose-dependent antifungal tolerance and establishes that tolerance is a dose-dependent phenomenon in C. auris.

title: Intracity-scale study reveals spatiotemporal variation of urban airborne microbiota and dynamics of antibiotic resistance/virulence genes
abstract: Airborne microbiota are critical to urban air quality and public health, yet their spatiotemporal differentiation, community assembly, and profiles of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factor genes (VFGs) across urban functional zones remain poorly characterized. In this study, monthly 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing was combined with seasonal metagenomic profiling of 12 composite samples and environmental data to investigate airborne microbiota at three sites representing commercial, industrial, and recreational zones in Changsha, China. Airborne communities showed similar spatial patterns among the investigated functional zones but strong seasonal variation, with Shannon diversity below 2.0 in July and above 6.0 in January. Proteobacteria dominated most samples, while key seasonal taxa shifted among Delftia, Cupriavidus, and Achromobacter. Neutral community modeling supported stochastic dominance (R= 0.664, Nm = 1,200), with 92.6% of operational taxonomic units within the 95% confidence interval. However, βNTI and RCbray analyses indicated increased deterministic selection in autumn-winter, coinciding with high pressure and pollutant accumulation. Metagenomics identified 25 ARG, 14 VFG, and 6 mobile genetic element (MGE) categories, with season explaining 53.9% of VFG compositional differences. Exploratory structural equation modeling identified associations between MGE abundance and ARG/VFG abundances (β = 0.75 and 1.09, respectively; both P < 0.001). Binning and contig co-localization showed that ARG-VFG-MGE co-harboring fragments were potentially affiliated with opportunistic pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae, indicating potential biosafety concerns.
