These findings identify season as a key driver of urban airborne microbiota and genetic risk factors, providing a basis for atmospheric biosafety monitoring and assessment.

title: Accelerated Laboratory Evolution Generates Growth-Costly High-Transfer Variants of an mcr-1-Bearing IncI2 Resistance Plasmid
abstract: This study aimed to characterize the plasmid-associated changes and host fitness consequences accompanying experimentally enriched high-transfer variants of the mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid p14E1050. We established an Accelerated Laboratory Evolution (ALE) system that coupled pMP6-mediated mutagenesis with iterative selection for enhanced conjugation frequency of the mcr-1-bearing p14E1050. Evolved lineages were characterized using conjugation assays, plasmid copy number (PCN) quantification, growth curve measurement, RNA-seq, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Under selection for plasmid transmissibility, the mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid p14E1050 rapidly evolved an enhanced conjugation phenotype, exhibiting a 41.05 ± 14.77-fold increase in conjugation frequency. WGS identified 32 mutations within the plasmid backbone of evolved variants. Increased PCN was associated with elevated conjugation frequency, while transcriptomic analysis of independent high-transfer variants revealed shared host-plasmid transcriptional remodeling, including upregulation of conjugation-related genes and pathways involved in nucleotide metabolism. Notably, enhanced transmissibility was accompanied by reduced host growth performance, indicating a cost to host-plasmid compatibility. Accelerated laboratory evolution rapidly enriched high-transfer variants of the mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid p14E1050, accompanied by increased PCN and reduced host growth. These findings suggest that high-transfer states can emerge during accelerated plasmid evolution, highlighting the relevance of evolutionary accessibility when evaluating antimicrobial resistance (AMR) plasmid dissemination risk.

title: MCR-Mediated Colistin Resistance Across the One Health Continuum in South Asia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Colistin remains a last-resort antibiotic for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, yet mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) genes threaten its continued utility. South Asia is a recognized hotspot for antimicrobial resistance, but the magnitude and distribution of MCR-mediated resistance across human, animal, food, and environmental sources in the region remain poorly characterized. We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO CRD420261414120). Five databases were searched without date restriction. Study proportions were pooled using a random-effects binomial-normal generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a logit link, the pre-specified primary analysis; the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation with the DerSimonian-Laird estimator was used as a sensitivity comparison. Subgroup analyses were performed by country, setting, and publication period. Risk of bias was assessed using the JBI prevalence checklist. Thirty-four data points (7,407 isolates; 1,243 MCR-positive) from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and India were included, drawn from 31 unique studies. Using the GLMM, the pooled MCR prevalence was 14.70% (95% CI 13.37-16.13%; I² ≈ 97.8%). The results remain unchanged when re-estimated with the Freeman-Tukey/DerSimonian-Laird sensitivity method (14.94%; 95% CI 7.98-23.49%). Bangladesh showed the highest country-level prevalence (37.34%; 95% CI 34.93-39.81%), while India showed the lowest (1.68%; 95% CI 0.98-2.86%). The animal and food compartment carried higher prevalence (35.69%; 95% CI 33.51-37.93%) than the clinical (3.87%; 95% CI 2.90-5.13%). mcr-1 was identified in 31 of 34 data points (91%). A directional temporal increase across successive publication periods reached statistical significance under GLMM-based logistic meta-regression (odds ratio 1.10 per year, 95% CI 1.06-1.15; p<0.001). MCR-mediated colistin resistance is widely disseminated across South Asia and disproportionately concentrated in the animal-food reservoir. Coordinated One Health surveillance and regulatory action on colistin use in livestock are urgently needed.

title: Corn-straw biochar modulates antibiotic resistance gene accumulation during swine manure composting: Insights into the role of dissolved organic matter transformation
abstract: Biochar has been reported to influence antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dynamics during livestock manure composting, but the role of dissolved organic matter (DOM) remains unclear. We investigated how DOM transformation was related to ARG dynamics during pig manure composting amended with corn-straw biochar. Biochar lowered dissolved organic carbon mainly during the early and middle stages, reduced specific ultraviolet absorbance at 254 nm from day 4 onward, and altered fluorescent DOM composition. ARG and mobile genetic element (MGE) relative abundances showed stage-dependent treatment differences: ARG relative abundance was higher with biochar on day 4 but lower on day 28, whereas MGE relative abundance was lower on day 28. Partial least squares path modeling showed that bacterial community composition had the strongest negative association with ARG abundance, whereas MGEs showed a positive association. A negative indirect association between biochar and ARG abundance involving bacterial community composition was partly offset by a positive DOM-related indirect association, resulting in a weak overall biochar-ARG association (0.04). These findings demonstrate stage-specific, rather than consistently suppressive, responses of ARGs and MGEs to biochar amendment and highlight linked statistical relationships among DOM, bacterial communities, MGEs, and ARGs rather than a single DOM-mediated mechanism.

title: Quantifying environment-dependent global antibiotic resistance gene risk patterns and mitigation scenarios using integrated machine learning and counterfactual scenario evaluation
abstract: Environmental antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) pose major ecological and public health risks, yet environmentally conditioned risk patterns and mitigation potential remain poorly quantified. This study aimed to characterize global ARG risk patterns, identify associated environmental and agricultural factors, and evaluate potential mitigation scenarios using an integrated machine learning framework. Using 274,382 sample-ARG-environment records and 150 environmental and agricultural variables, quantile models characterized conditional risk index (RI) distributions and upper-tail risks, multi-model analysis assessed predictive variable importance, and DML estimated covariate-adjusted conditional associations. Heterogeneity was assessed across habitats, countries, and ARG categories, followed by directionally constrained counterfactual evaluation of multi-factor mitigation scenarios. Global ARG risk varied strongly with environmental conditions. In predictive importance analyses, winter temperature anomalies, manure nutrient loading, and pesticide application were important for upper-tail RI prediction. Separately, DML identified positive conditional associations of RI with insecticide application, cropland nutrient surplus, and manure loading, and negative associations with nutrient use efficiency. These associations varied across habitats, particularly soil, crop roots, freshwater, and biological waste environments. Under a predefined 50% predicted RI reduction target, nine-factor adjustment reduced mean standardized adjustment distance by 69.1% relative to single-factor adjustment, although outcomes varied among ARG categories. These model-based findings support global ARG risk characterization and management prioritization within the One Health framework, subject to empirical validation.

title: Advances in the management of pneumonia caused by drug-resistant bacteria: from antimicrobial optimisation to integrated treatment adaptation
abstract: Management of drug-resistant bacterial pneumonia has become increasingly precise, but early precision does not remove the need to reinterpret the patient's course during illness. Active and appropriate empirical therapy, informed by local epidemiology, remains essential, yet treatment often begins before the definitive microbiological profile is available or adequate drug exposure can be confirmed. While rapid diagnostics and pharmacological optimisation can narrow this initial uncertainty, the harder problem arises when antimicrobial treatment appears plausible but the patient shows delayed improvement, clinical deterioration, or incomplete recovery. These trajectories should not be treated as a single form of antibiotic failure. Instead, they require reassessment of whether the dominant limitation is persistent infection, inadequate drug exposure, dysregulated host response, a non-infectious mimic, or repair-limited recovery. In this Review, we propose a trajectory-guided conceptual framework that links management to the process most likely to limit recovery and distinguishes clinically implementable interventions from emerging translational concepts.

title: Identification of peptide epitopes in major antigens of Yersinia pestis from infected humans and immunised mice
abstract: Yersinia pestis (Y. pestis), the bacterial pathogen responsible for plague in humans, remains a public health threat, particularly in light of the recent emergence of antibiotic resistance strains. To better understand the immune response against plague and to identify potential targets for immunointervention, we performed an epitope mapping study of the IgG response against a library of peptides representing 18 Y. pestis proteins. The study included sera from 51 individuals who had recovered from plague, 26 uninfected human controls, and 20 sera from mice protected by a live-attenuated vaccine. Analysis of human sera revealed 32 reactive peptides distributed across eight protein antigens, whereas analysis of mouse sera identified 187 reactive peptides spanning all 18 proteins. Combined analysis of the human and mouse IgG responses to the 32 human-reactive peptides identified 27 B-cell epitopes located within YopD, YopB, LcrV, FyuA, Pla, Ail, Caf1, and PsaA. Of these, one epitope had previously been described as protective and another as immunodominant, whereas the remaining 25 represent immunodominant epitopes identified in this study. Interestingly, IgG antibody responses to selected YopD and YopB peptides were significantly stronger in pneumonic plague than in bubonic plague, suggesting that the distinct clinical manifestations of the disease may be associated with distinct underlying pathophysiological and molecular mechanisms. Our comprehensive mapping of linear IgG epitopes recognised by convalescent human sera, combined with prioritisation based on their predicted neutralising potential, provides a resource for future studies evaluating peptide-based diagnostics, vaccines, and monoclonal antibody therapies against plague. The project was supported by a grant from Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR).

title: Surveillance of high-priority enterococci and factors associated with clinical enterococcal infections in a Reference Hospital in northern Nigeria
abstract: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) are high-priority pathogens; however, most healthcare providers in resource-limited settings do not consider enterococci in the differential diagnosis of clinical bacterial infections. This cross-sectional surveillance study determined the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profile of Enterococcus and factors associated with their presence in patients attending the Ahmadu Bello University Teaching Hospital (ABUTH), Zaria, Nigeria. Non-repetitive clinical samples from 180 patients were processed for the isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing of enterococci in Slanetz-Bartley agar and the Vitek® 2 Compact system. Structured questionnaires were used to collect participants' sociodemographic and risk factor data. The prevalence of enterococcal infection was 23.3% (42/180), comprising 57.1% Enterococcus faecalis and 42.9% Enterococcus faecium. Subgroup analysis showed no significant association between the isolation rates and sample type (p=0.379). The frequency of enterococcal infection was significantly highest among patients aged 31-40 years (p<0.05), with a higher frequency among older patients. Moreover, unemployed patients (OR=1.8, p=0.0195) and those using pit latrines (OR=2.1, p=0.034) had significantly increased the odds of enterococcal infection. Enterococci resistance was highest against ampicillin (100%), tetracycline (90.5%), and ciprofloxacin (69%), with 83.3% exhibiting a multidrug-resistant (MDR) phenotype. Remarkably, 7.1% of all isolates were VR-E. faecium. Moreover, enterococci with a multiple antimicrobial resistance (MAR) index of 0.3 (45.2%) were predominant. A high level of MDR enterococci (including VRE) was identified in the clinical samples from patients initially managed for non-enterococcal infections, underscoring the need to use a selective bacteriological medium to minimize microbiological misdiagnosis in resource-limited healthcare settings. This study provides valuable local surveillance data indicating gaps in the integration of appropriate diagnostic bacteriology into clinical infectious disease practice.

title: Nanorobots Are Using Light and Clever Engineering to Beat Biofilms and Tackle Antimicrobial-Resistant Infections
abstract: The scope of the antimicrobial resistance issue is huge-one promising solution may be much, much smaller. In thisarticle, JMIR Correspondent Liam Critchley reports on advances in micro/nanorobotics, which may provide new avenues for treating biofilm infections.

title: Engineering smart liposomes to combat antimicrobial resistance: from mechanistic design to clinical translation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health threat, surpassing the pace of discovery and clinical development of new antimicrobial agents. Therefore, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to enhance antibiotic efficacy, overcome multidrug-resistant infections, and limit resistance development. Smart liposomal nanoplatforms have emerged as promising tools capable of improving antimicrobial therapy through targeted delivery, enhanced bacterial uptake, biofilm penetration, protection against enzymatic degradation, and controlled drug release. This review examines recent advances in the rational design of evolved liposomes, including stimuli-responsive and programmable systems, for combating resistant bacterial infections. It discusses their ability to improve pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, overcome biological barriers, and enable precision antimicrobial delivery. Current translational challenges, including large-scale manufacturing, physicochemical characterization, regulatory requirements, and clinically relevant preclinical models, are critically evaluated. Emerging strategies, such as artificial intelligence-driven formulation optimization, continuous microfluidic manufacturing, multifunctional therapeutic platforms incorporating gene editing, and next-generation antibiotic-adjuvant combination strategies, are also explored. Liposomal drug-delivery systems may improve the exposure, distribution, and intracellular or local delivery of antimicrobial agents, but improved delivery should not be equated with reversal of bacterial resistance. Successful clinical translation will depend on formulation- and infection-specific evidence, clinically relevant preclinical models, controlled and scalable manufacturing, and appropriate regulatory frameworks, while artificial intelligence, digital-twin, and precision-medicine approaches are best viewed as decision-support tools that complement experimental and clinical validation.

title: Lateral opening site of human oligopeptide transporter 2 plays a key role in the interaction with polymyxins
abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria pose a critical global health threat, while polymyxins remain a last-line therapy. However, their clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity. Human oligopeptide transporter 2 (hPepT2) is a membrane transporter mediating the reabsorption of polymyxins in renal cells and contributes to their nephrotoxicity, but the molecular basis of their interaction remains unclear. Here, we investigated the structure-interaction relationship (SIR) of polymyxins with hPepT2 by integrating computational, chemical, and cell biology approaches. Bioinformatic modeling predicted an outward-facing hPepT2 structure and a potential transport pathway, with polymyxins interacting at the lateral opening, particularly E214, D215, D317, D342, and E622. Transporter mutagenesis and molecular analyses confirmed that D215 is critical for polymyxin binding, while other residues influence transporter turnover and/or expression. We subsequently synthesized polymyxin analogs with modifications at Dab1, Dab3, Dab5, and Dab9 of polymyxins, which reduced interactions with hPepT2. Notably, alanine substitution at Dab3 reduced nephrotoxicity in mice while retaining antibacterial activity. Overall, this proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the hPepT2-polymyxin SIR model provides a viable strategy for developing novel, safer lipopeptide antibiotics.

title: Repurposing Etravirine as a PlcA-Targeting inhibitor to block autophagic escape of Listeria monocytogenes
abstract: The rapid rise of antibiotic resistance underscores the urgent need for anti-infective strategies that circumvent classical bactericidal approaches. Host-directed antivirulence therapies, which target host defense pathways or pathogen virulence rather than essential viability, may reduce selection pressure and delay resistance, but potent small-molecule examples remain limited. Here we identified a drug repurposing candidate against the intracellular pathogen() by targeting its phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C PlcA, a key virulence factor involved in autophagy escape. Using a compound-microarray high-throughput binding platform, we discovered that the approved HIV non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor Etravirine directly bound PlcA and inhibited its phosphatidylinositol-hydrolyzing activity without affecting bacterial growth ortranscription. In infected cells, Etravirine restored PtdIns3P levels, increased MAP1LC3/LC3 (microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3) recruitment and autophagic flux, promoted lysosomal delivery, and reduced infection-induced cellular damage. Etravirine also enhanced basal autophagic flux and induced an autophagy-associated transcriptional program. These effects were reproduced in RAW264.7 macrophages and were attenuated by 3-MA. In mouse infection models, Etravirine reduced bacterial burdens and inflammatory pathology and improved survival. Biophysical, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), docking, mutational, and preliminary analogue analyses supported a putative Etravirine-binding region near the PlcA myo-inositol-binding pocket. Together, these findings establish Etravirine as a PlcA-targeting antivirulence candidate that also strengthens host autophagy-associated restriction of.

title: Amoxicillin removal by babassu-derived activated carbon under ultrasonic irradiation: adsorption performance and tree-based machine learning modeling
abstract: The contamination of aquatic environments by antibiotics has become a major environmental concern due to their persistence and contribution to antimicrobial resistance. In this study, activated carbon derived from babassu endocarp (BAC) was evaluated for the removal of amoxicillin (AMX) from aqueous solutions under ultrasonic irradiation. BAC exhibited a heterogeneous porous structure with a specific surface area of 623.38 m g. Adsorption equilibrium was achieved within approximately 10 min under ultrasonic irradiation. This equilibrium time is shorter than equilibrium times reported for many activated carbons used for AMX removal. The Freundlich model provided the best fit to the equilibrium data, while the Langmuir model predicted a maximum adsorption capacity of 185.57 mg g. Thermodynamic analysis indicated that the adsorption process was spontaneous and endothermic. BAC also maintained satisfactory adsorption performance after four regeneration cycles. In addition, tree-based machine learning algorithms, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), and Extra Trees (ET), were applied to predict adsorption capacity, with the ET model achieving the best predictive performance (R = 0.983) in the test dataset. Feature importance analysis identified the initial AMX concentration as the most influential operational variable. The adsorption mechanism was proposed to involve pore filling, hydrogen bonding, π-π interactions, and electrostatic attractions. Overall, the results demonstrate that BAC is a promising low-cost adsorbent for rapid AMX removal and highlight the applicability of machine-learning approaches for adsorption process prediction.

title: Group A streptococcus vaccine strategies: virulence targets, resistance constraints and complementary control measures
abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

title: Comparison of secondary metabolite profiles of Bacillus licheniformis produced on conventional and cheese-waste-based media: antimicrobial activity and GC-MS analysis
abstract: Bacteria of the genus Bacillus attract interest for their ability to produce secondary metabolites with important biotechnological and biomedical applications. Metabolites produced by thermophilic strains, however, have received far less attention and remain poorly characterised. In the context of increasing antibiotic resistance and growing pressure to limit chemical inputs, particularly in agriculture, there is a pressing need to identify new bio-based antimicrobial compounds. Additionally, using inexpensive substrates could reduce production costs. Thermophilic B. licheniformis strain LMB3G52 was grown on two different substrates: conventional Luria-Bertani (LB) medium and an innovative medium derived from cheese waste. This strain showed broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity that was significantly stronger in LB medium. Chloroform extracts inhibited Acinetobacter baumannii (19.7 ± 0.6 mm) and Listeria monocytogenes (18 ± 1 mm). GC-MS revealed distinct substrate-dependent metabolite profiles: cheese waste medium predominantly yielded hexadecanoic acid methyl ester (31.0%) and octadecanoic acid methyl ester (28.4%), whereas the LB-medium extract was dominated by a compound putatively identified, from NIST library matching, as dimethyl phthalate (52.0%). LB-derived extracts showed enhanced antifungal activity, with mycelial growth inhibition of 80.7 ± 0.6% (Penicillium sp.) and 70 ± 1.4% (A. parasiticus). To our knowledge, this is the first report of putatively identified dimethyl phthalate as a major constituent of B. licheniformis extracts, although its precise biosynthetic route remains to be confirmed. Our work also demonstrates that cheese processing effluent can serve as a low-cost alternative substrate for antimicrobial compound production. These findings contribute to both microbial metabolite discovery and sustainable valorisation of dairy waste.

title: [Group B Streptococcus colonization in pregnant women, neonatal bacteremia, and antimicrobial resistance profile in a maternity hospital in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic]
A temperate phage acts as a symbiotic fitness enhancer for UPEC but surrenders to combination therapy through lysogeny suppression
abstract: Temperate phages are increasingly recognized as key drivers of bacterial evolution. Here, we isolated a myoviral prophage, vB_EcoM_P899, from a clinical uropathogenic(UPEC) isolate and characterized how lysogenization shapes host biology. Lysogenization significantly enhanced biofilm formation, swarming motility, oxidative stress resistance, and adhesion to macrophages (up to 100-fold) without altering antibiotic susceptibility or overall 72-h lethality in thelarval infection model. Mechanistically, this is associated with upregulation of the fimbrial geneand enhanced inducibility of the oxidative stress response genesandunder oxidative stress. Crucially, combining P899 with ciprofloxacin or kanamycin produced synergistic killing and suppressed new lysogen formation in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. In contrast, ceftazidime, while synergistic, failed to prevent lysogeny. Our findings demonstrate that while prophage vB_EcoM_P899 promotes bacterial niche adaptation, its lysogenization frequency is significantly reduced under specific antibiotic pressure, facilitating clearance of the challenged UPEC population. This work provides a strong rationale for optimizing phage-antibiotic combination therapies to treat drug-resistant infections by simultaneously enhancing bacterial killing and limiting lysogenic survivors. This study reveals that lysogenization by a temperate phage can enhance the niche adaptation of uropathogenicwithout increasing its virulence in thelarval model or altering antibiotic resistance. Crucially, we demonstrate that combining this phage with select antibiotics (e.g., kanamycin and ciprofloxacin) not only kills the bacteria effectively but also actively suppresses the formation of new lysogens in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. These findings uncover a novel role for temperate phages as symbiotic regulators within the host and provide direct experimental evidence for a phage-antibiotic combination strategy. This approach holds promise for combating chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections and offers a clinically viable pathway to address antibiotic tolerance in chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections.

title: Adjunctive recombinant human thymosin β4 therapy improves antibacterial outcomes against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) is an endogenous multifunctional protein with growing therapeutic applications, including infectious diseases; however, its intrinsic antibacterial activity remains unclear. Previous research with the peptide and related shellfish homologs has suggested broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties, including activity against. Here, we evaluated the antibacterial activity of recombinant human Tβ4 (rhTβ4) alone and in combination with antibiotics againststrain 8325-4 and two clinical isolates. Direct antibacterial activity of rhTβ4 (15.625-16,000 µg/mL) was assessed by broth microdilution and colony-forming unit enumeration. Interactions between rhTβ4 and antibiotics were evaluated using checkerboard assays examining total, planktonic, and biofilm-associated bacterial populations. Biofilms were further analyzed using crystal violet staining and SYTO9/PI labeling to assess biomass and membrane integrity, respectively. Moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, oxacillin, and vancomycin were evaluated. rhTβ4 alone exhibited modest growth-modulating effects but lacked substantial direct antibacterial activity. In contrast, rhTβ4 demonstrated synergistic interactions with multiple antibiotics, resulting in reduced bacterial growth primarily within total and planktonic populations. Limited effects were observed against established biofilms, as rhTβ4 did not significantly reduce biofilm biomass or membrane integrity, and combination treatments produced antibiotic-dependent biofilm responses. Collectively, these findings indicate that rhTβ4 possesses little intrinsic antibacterial activity againstbut can synergistically augment the effects of select antibiotics, supporting its utility as an adjunctive therapeutic strategy.IMPORTANCEremains a leading cause of severe infections worldwide, and the rise in antibiotic resistance emphasizes the need for new therapeutic strategies. Thymosin β4 (Tβ4), a naturally occurring human peptide already known to promote tissue repair, may also enhance bacterial clearance. This study demonstrates that recombinant human Tβ4 exhibits direct growth-modulating activity againstand, more importantly, synergizes with multiple antibiotics to reduce bacterial growth. These findings suggest that Tβ4 could serve as an adjunctive therapy, improving the efficacy of conventional antibiotics while leveraging its immunomodulatory and wound-healing properties. By uncovering a potential antimicrobial dimension to a well-characterized endogenous peptide, this work broadens the therapeutic scope of Tβ4 and supports its further development as a novel strategy for treating antibiotic-resistant or biofilm-associated infections.

title: Drug Repurposing and Advanced Delivery Systems Targeting Multidrug-Resistant Microorganisms: A Narrative Review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, driven by the spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens alongside a declining antibiotic pipeline. Drug repurposing offers a cost-effective, time-efficient alternative by identifying antimicrobial applications for approved drugs with established safety profiles. Agents including auranofin, niclosamide, gallium compounds, phenothiazines, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, ticagrelor, and dronedarone show antimicrobial, antibiofilm, antivirulence, and resistance-modifying activity through mechanisms distinct from conventional antibiotics, potentially limiting cross-resistance. However, reported in vitro minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) frequently exceed clinical breakpoints and plasma concentrations achievable at approved doses, confining most candidates to adjuvant or local therapy rather than systemic monotherapy. Poor solubility, limited bioavailability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, and systemic toxicity further constrain clinical translation. Advanced drug delivery systems (DDS) like nanoparticles, liposomes, metal-organic frameworks, and stimuli-responsive carriers may mitigate these barriers by improving stability, targeting, infection-site accumulation, and controlled release. Such platforms can additionally enhance biofilm penetration, enable intracellular delivery, and permit co-delivery with conventional antibiotics to achieve synergy. Integrating repurposed agents with advanced DDS could therefore address key resistance mechanisms, including biofilm formation, efflux activity, and intracellular persistence, although substantial challenges remain despite encouraging preclinical data. This review critically evaluates the antimicrobial potential of repurposed non-antimicrobial drugs spanning anti-arthritic, anthelmintic, antineoplastic, psychiatric, and cardiovascular classes, examining mechanisms of action, efficacy evidence, and principal limitations, and assesses how advanced DDS might improve their therapeutic performance against MDR infections. It further identifies major evidence gaps and research priorities to guide development of clinically viable anti-AMR strategies.

title: Paper Strip-Based Sensor for Detection of Antimicrobial Resistant Listeria monocytogenes in Milk
abstract: To develop a rapid, selective, and field-deployable paper strip assay for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and targeted screening of resistance to Penicillin G and Ampicillin in milk. A novel Listeria Selective Enrichment Medium (LSEM) was optimized to enhance the recovery of L. monocytogenes in milk while reducing interference from selected competing microorganisms evaluated in this study. The assay employed β-D-glucosidase and enzyme-substrate reactions for presumptive and species-specific detection, producing characteristic colour changes for Listeria spp. The developed paper strip detected L. monocytogenes within 7 h in broth and 9 h (with enrichment for 24 h at 1 CFU/25 mL) in spiked sterilized milk. The total detection time of the developed assay was approximately 33 h (24 h enrichment + 9 h strip-based confirmation). In the present study, antimicrobial resistance assessment was limited to two representative β-lactam antibiotics, Penicillin G and Ampicillin. Therefore, the assay should currently be considered a targeted screening platform rather than a universal antimicrobial susceptibility test. Resistant strains showed colour development in the presence of the respective antibiotic, whereas susceptible strains remained colourless. Validation with 70 milk samples confirmed one raw milk sample positive for L. monocytogenes, which was further verified using ISO 11290-1:2017 and disc diffusion methods. The developed assay provides a rapid, selective, cost-effective, and user-friendly platform for simultaneous detection of L. monocytogenes and targeted susceptibility screening to Penicillin G and Ampicillin in milk.

title: A new validated UHPLC method for the simultaneous determination of diclofenac sodium and oxacillin sodium monohydrate for their combined dosage form for dermal delivery
abstract: The rising prevalence of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among biofilm-forming pathogens such as methicillin-resistant(MRSA), has intensified the need for therapeutic strategies capable of improving antibacterial efficacy against resistant infections. Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) exhibit limited intrinsic antimicrobial activity, growing evidence suggests that certain NSAIDs can potentiate conventional antibiotics, producing synergistic antibacterial and antibiofilm effects. Accordingly, the combined delivery of an NSAID and an antibiotic represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting infection-associated inflammation and bacterial persistence while potentially enhancing antibacterial activity. Incorporation of such drug combinations into nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) may further support topical delivery; however, reliable simultaneous quantification of both drugs within this complex lipid-based system remains analytically challenging. An ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography method with diode array detection (UHPLC-DAD) was developed and validated for the simultaneous quantification of oxacillin sodium monohydrate and diclofenac sodium in nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) intended for dermal delivery. Chromatographic separation was achieved on an XTerra MS C18 column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) using gradient elution with 0.05 M orthophosphoric acid in water and acetonitrile at a flow rate of 1.0 mL min, with detection at 210 nm. Oxacillin and diclofenac were baseline separated with retention times of 8.74 and 13.73 min, respectively. The method was validated in accordance with International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidelines and demonstrated linearity over the concentration range of 5-100 µg mLfor both analytes (≥ 0.9996). The limits of detection and quantification were 1.38 and 4.18 µg mLfor oxacillin, and 2.69 and 8.15 µg mLfor diclofenac, respectively. Precision was satisfactory, with intra-day and inter-day relative standard deviation values below 3%. Specificity was confirmed by the absence of matrix interference, while recovery studies demonstrated acceptable accuracy for both analytes in the formulation matrix. Under thermal (65 °C) and photolytic (405 nm) stress conditions, oxacillin showed recoveries of 81.16-97.77%, while diclofenac showed recoveries of 84.92-93.50%, indicating reduced recovery following stress exposure. The proposed method is reliable for the routine quantification of both drugs in dual-drug lipid-based formulations and is applicable to quality control, formulation development, and permeation studies.

title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation
abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

title: Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis
abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

title: Gram-Negative Bacterial Resistance
abstract: The rapid worldwide spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacteria is driven by a complex interplay of human, environmental, and health care-associated factors and accelerated by mobile genetic elements that facilitate the dissemination of resistance genes. Resistance in gram-negative bacteria arises primarily through reduced drug entry, active drug efflux, modification of antibiotic targets, and enzymatic drug inactivation, most notably through β-lactamase production. Clinically important resistant pathogens include extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales,with difficult-to-treat resistance, and carbapenem-resistant. Limited access to effective antibiotics and the continued emergence of resistance to available agents pose substantial challenges to the management of these infections. Appropriate management requires timely and accurate diagnostics, targeted use of newer β-lactam agents, effective source control, and judicious selection of treatment durations.

title: Tire-derived 6PPD-quinone promotes conjugative gene transfer through respiratory bioenergetic perturbation
abstract: Tire-derived N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone (6PPD-Q) is transported by roadway runoff into urban waters, yet its sublethal effects on microbial gene exchange remain poorly resolved. Here, 5 μg/L 6PPD-Q increased the transconjugant fraction from 0.25% to 0.65% in a lake-water enriched biofilm community and enhanced plasmid transfer in a defined donor-recipient system. Relative to its parent compound 6PPD, 6PPD-Q more strongly altered oxidative phosphorylation, ATP/ADP ratios, and NAD/NADH balance. Molecular simulations indicated membrane partitioning and predicted quinone-site interactions resembling those of ubiquinone analogues, while cyclic voltammetry and partial growth rescue of a ubiB-deficient strain supported quinone-associated redox activity. 6PPD-Q also increased succinate dehydrogenase activity, oxygen consumption, membrane potential, and ATP/ADP ratios. Respiratory-chain and bioenergetic inhibitors attenuated both these responses and the transfer enhancement, linking the phenotype to cellular energy metabolism. Extracellular filament-like structures, migration responses, and appendage-related transcription changed concurrently, although the structures could not be assigned to a specific pilus system. These results support respiratory bioenergetic perturbation as an upstream contributor to 6PPD-Q-enhanced conjugation and identify microbial gene exchange as a water-quality endpoint relevant to tire-contaminated runoff and receiving waters.

title: Cascading effects of nano-biochar mitigate antibiotic resistance via phage-host interactions in the soil-crop ecosystem
abstract: Controlling the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in agroecosystems is central to One Health, yet whether nano-biochar-amended organic fertilizers can mitigate phage-mediated ARG dissemination along the fertilizer-soil-crop continuum remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 120 viral metagenomes to examine how biochar-amended organic fertilizers modulate ARG dynamics, phage-associated functions, and phage-host interactions across the fertilizer-soil-lettuce continuum. The lettuce phyllosphere served as a key endpoint for ARG accumulation, exhibiting 4.1-4.9 times the total ARG abundance and 56.8-66.3% higher phage-encoded ARG abundance compared with rhizosphere and non-rhizosphere soils. Source-tracking analysis indicated that manure and soil inputs accounted for 50.8-57.0% of phyllosphere ARGs, while 111 manure-associated viral populations were shared with the phyllosphere at the viral cluster level. Notably, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost exerted a cascading mitigation effect, reducing manure- and soil-derived ARG inputs to the phyllosphere by 20.4-21.6% and manure-associated viral sharing by 51.6%. Meanwhile, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost reduced lysogenic phage-host interactions, phage-encoded ARGs, and auxiliary metabolic genes associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which may contribute to reduced phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. Consequently, total ARG abundance in the phyllosphere decreased by 68.9-76.3%, while lettuce biomass increased by 54.1-61.5%. This work suggests that nano-biochar-amended vermicompost may mitigate antibiotic resistance risks and enhance crop productivity partly by attenuating phage-associated ARG dissemination across the fertilizer-soil-crop continuum, highlighting its potential for One Health-oriented resistance-risk control in agricultural production.

title: External validation of the MDR score for predicting multidrug-resistant device-associated infections in pediatric intensive care units (PEPE-MDR score): a nationwide registry-based study
abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms are an increasing cause of device-associated healthcare-associated infections (DA-HAIs) in pediatric intensive care units (PICUs), complicating empirical antibiotic selection. The aim of the study was to externally validate the MDR-score (PEPE-MDR score), a tool developed to estimate the likelihood of a DA-HAI being caused by MDR. A multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted using surveillance data from the pediatric ENVIN-HELICS registry (2014-2024). Pediatric patients with microbiologically confirmed DA-HAIs were included. The PEPE-MDR score incorporates prior MDR colonization, comorbidity, and PICU length of stay > 9 days. Discrimination was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), sensitivity, specificity, and positive (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV). Calibration was evaluated with the observed-to-expected (O:E) ratio and the calibration slope. Among 21,999 episodes registered, 406 DA-HAIs were included. Of these, 93 (22.9%) were caused by MDR organisms. Median (IQR) MDR scores were higher in MDR infections than non-MDR infections (p < 0.001), with a Hodges-Lehmann location shift (95% CI) of 3 points (2-4). The MDR score yielded an AUC-ROC of 0.69 (95% CI 0.62-0.75). Using the high-risk category as the threshold, sensitivity and specificity were 46.2% and 79.9% (PPV 40.6%; NPV 83.3%). Combining moderate- and high-risk categories increased sensitivity to 77.4% with specificity 47.0% (PPV 30.3%; NPV 87.5%). Observed risks were lower than predicted: O:E ratio 0.64 (95% CI 0.54-0.77), although risk increased across categories (12.5%, 22.0%, 40.6%; p < 0.001).  In this multicenter external validation, the PEPE-MDR score provided moderate discrimination and preserved risk stratification for MDR DA-HAIs, contributing to empirical antibiotic decision-making in PICUs after recalibration to local prevalence. • Acknowledging the risk of a multidrug resistant microorganism involvement in infections related to invasive devices is crucial to adjust empirical antibiotherapy in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). • A MDR score for Predicting Multidrug-Resistant Device-Associated Infections in Pediatric Intensive Care Units (PEPE-MDR score) was developed recently, but it required external validation. • The PEPE-MDR score was validated in a multicenter national database. • These findings support the PEPE-MDR score's utility as a practical tool for adjusting empirical antibiotic treatment in the PICU setting.

title: Constructing a Perspective of Probiotic Bacteria in the Management of Urinary Tract Infection in Cats: A Scoping Review
authors: de Lima Núñez TA et al.
abstract: Feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD) and urinary tract infections (UTIs) pose a significant clinical challenge in companion animal medicine. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and emerging insights into the feline urinary microbiome highlight the potential of probiotic-based therapeutic strategies. However, the scope and quality of existing evidence in feline medicine remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically map and characterize the literature on probiotic microorganisms (particularly Lactobacillus spp. and Bifidobacterium spp.) in feline urinary health, identifying research domains, evidence gaps, and future priorities. A scoping review identified peer-reviewed studies addressing FLUTD, urinary microbiota, antimicrobial resistance, and probiotic interventions. Studies were categorized into four domains: clinical burden, microbiome evidence, clinical probiotic evidence, and mechanistic probiotic evidence. Fifty-three studies met inclusion criteria. The main finding of this review is that there is limited to no direct evidence on the use of probiotics for the management of FLUTD or UTIs in cats: only nine studies addressed probiotics (clinical probiotic evidence: n = 5; mechanistic probiotic evidence: n = 4), and no randomized controlled trials specifically assessing probiotic efficacy in cats were identify. Most literature focused on clinical burden (n = 37), comprising epidemiological surveys and antimicrobial resistance reports, whereas microbiome investigations were limited (n = 7). The high prevalence of Escherichia coli and increasing antimicrobial resistance underscore the need for alternative strategies. Addressing this gap through well-designed clinical trials in cats is essential before probiotic-based strategies can be recommended to improve both clinical outcomes and animal welfare in feline patients.

title: Detection of high-risk sequence type ST131 among multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli causing urinary tract infections in Cusco, Peru
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli represents a growing public health challenge, particularly in urinary tract infections (UTIs), where this pathogen remains the leading etiological agent. The emergence of multidrug-resistant strains producing extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) and carbapenemases has markedly limited therapeutic options and promoted the persistence of high-risk lineages in hospital settings. In this study, phenotypic, molecular, and genomic characterization were conducted on 50 multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli isolates obtained from urine cultures of patients treated at the Regional Hospital of Cusco, Peru. ESBL and carbapenemase production were assessed using standardised phenotypic methods, while resistance genes were detected by endpoint PCR. For genomic characterization, MDR E. coli isolates (RUE 08 and RUE 29) were selected from the panel of 50 isolates. These were chosen as representative samples for whole-genome sequencing and comparative genomic analysis. All isolates were confirmed as ESBL producers, and 40% exhibited carbapenemase production. The detected genes were bla(94%), bla(36%), bla(2%), bla(26%), bla(20%) and blawas not detected. The detection of blaand blarepresents the first documented report of these genes in multidrug-resistant E. coli in the city of Cusco. Genomic analysis identified the high-risk lineage ST131 in one sequenced isolate, characterised by an extensive repertoire of virulence and resistance genes associated with the ExPEC/UPEC pathotype, as well as a second isolate belonging to ST361, which harboured clinically relevant resistance genes but displayed a limited virulence profile. These findings demonstrate the circulation of clinically relevant multidrug-resistant E. coli in southern Peru and underscore the need to strengthen molecular surveillance through the incorporation of genomic tools to enable early detection of high-risk clones and support effective antimicrobial control strategies.

title: Carbon dot/TiO(2) nanocomposites for photocatalytic antibiotic degradation: interfacial engineering, degradation mechanisms, and environmental remediation
abstract: The widespread presence of antibiotic residues in aquatic environments contributes to ecological toxicity and accelerates antimicrobial resistance (AMR), highlighting the need for efficient and sustainable remediation technologies. Among advanced oxidation processes, TiO-based photocatalysis has attracted considerable attention because of its chemical stability, low toxicity, and strong oxidative capability. However, the practical application of TiOis limited by poor visible-light absorption and rapid electron-hole recombination. Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as highly promising interfacial modifiers owing to their tunable electronic structure, visible-light responsiveness, and efficient charge-transfer capability, enabling substantial enhancement of TiOphotocatalytic performance. This review critically examines recent advances in CDs/TiOnanocomposites for photocatalytic antibiotic degradation, with particular emphasis on how heterointerface engineering governs charge-carrier dynamics, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and degradation selectivity. The mechanistic roles of Ti-O-C interfacial bonding, band alignment, defect-state modulation, and interfacial electron transfer are systematically discussed in relation to photocatalytic activity across major antibiotic classes, including tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, β-lactams, and sulfonamides. In addition, the effects of adsorption behavior, operational parameters, environmental matrix components, and reactor configuration on degradation efficiency and mineralization are critically evaluated. Special attention is devoted to degradation pathways, catalyst photostability, ecotoxicological considerations, and challenges associated with real-water applications and large-scale implementation. Current limitations, including insufficient mechanistic validation, lack of standardized benchmarking protocols, and limited long-term environmental safety assessment, are also highlighted. Finally, current research priorities involving mechanistic validation, predictive interfacial engineering, standardized benchmarking, environmental safety assessment, and solar-driven photocatalytic design are highlighted to guide the future development of sustainable antibiotic-remediation technologies.

title: Bacteriophages versus priority pathogens: resistance mechanisms, therapeutic challenges, and opportunities for novel combinations
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a critical global health threat, and renewed interest in bacteriophage (phage) therapy highlights its potential as a targeted alternative to antibiotic monotherapy. However, phage resistance in bacteria remains a key limiting factor in phage therapy, driven by evolutionary adaptations to phage exposure. Antibacterial modalities (antibiotics, adjuvants, antimicrobial peptides, and RNA-based therapeutics) could help overcome these barriers and represent untapped potential for synergistic, precision antimicrobial interventions when combined with phage therapy. Importantly, bacterial physiology and environmental context could strongly influence treatment outcomes, underscoring the need for clinically relevant models for testing combinations. Integration of multi-omics and artificial intelligence-driven approaches could help predict patterns for the development of precision therapies and support the development of novel antimicrobial interventions.

title: Plague in the modern world: Ecological persistence, epidemic containment, and the limits of public health preparedness
abstract: Yersinia pestis persists across sylvatic rodent-flea reservoirs globally and is not currently amenable to eradication. Paleogenomic and paleoecological evidence indicates that historical plague pandemics reflected complex interactions among pathogen biology, environmental conditions, and societal vulnerabilities rather than pathogen virulence alone. Drawing a qualified epidemiological comparison to cholera, contemporary public health interventions show that effective disease control does not necessarily require eliminating a pathogen from its natural reservoirs; for plague, modern clinical and public health measures have substantially decoupled zoonotic spillovers from pandemic amplification. Whereas cholera control relies predominantly on water and sanitation barriers alongside clinical, vaccination, and surveillance programs, plague containment depends primarily on zoonotic monitoring, rapid diagnosis, early antimicrobial therapy, and contact management. The October 2026 unexplained fatal pneumonia in a Russian anti-plague laboratory worker illustrates both the capacity and the limitations of outbreak surveillance when targeted assays reported by national authorities are negative but etiology remains unresolved. With 97.7% of the 2646 confirmed human cases reported globally during 2019-2025 concentrated in two endemic countries, sustaining containment requires addressing healthcare inequities, maintaining clinical vigilance, monitoring antimicrobial resistance, and enforcing rigorous biosafety.

title: Shotgun Metagenomic Profiling of Phlebotomus papatasi (Diptera: Psychodidae, Phlebotomine) in Zoonotic Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Endemic Foci of Iraq: Microbiota, Resistome, and Virulome
abstract: This study aims to develop a regional baseline for future individual-level and comparative studies of microbial ecology and symbiont-based vector control. Phlebotomus papatasi is a major vector of Leishmania major and an important component of the transmission cycle of zoonotic cutaneous leishmaniasis (ZCL) in Iraq, although the internal microbial communities of this vector are poorly characterised in the region. In this study, shotgun metagenomic sequencing was employed to investigate the microbial communities of a pooled sample of 129 blood-fed female Ph. papatasi collected from ZCL-endemic foci in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq, from 2024 to 2025. Approximately 32.9 million raw reads were obtained from sequencing, with the quality-filtered, host-removed, and low-diversity-filtered reads analysed for taxonomic and functional profiles. The data revealed a complex microbial community inside blood-fed Ph. papatasi dominated by bacteria. Moreover, several species of Proteobacteria in blood-fed Ph. papatasi were detected, which accounted for 98.32% of the classified reads, with Enterobacter cloacae as the most common species (74.34% of classified reads). Strains associated with Wolbachia were also detected (approximately 8.96% of classified reads). The microbial data further revealed the presence of genes associated with antimicrobial resistance including oqxA/oqxB-associated efflux and AmpC-type β-lactamase families, and virulence factors associated with motility, iron acquisition, and secretion systems. Nevertheless, the data represented the distribution of sequencing reads within the pooled sample (single sample), rather than the prevalence or average abundance among individual sand flies.

title: In vitro activity of imipenem/relebactam against Enterobacterales isolates from China: results from the Study of Monitoring Antimicrobial Resistance Trends (SMART), 2020-2022
abstract: Imipenem/relebactam (IMR) is a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that enhances the activity of imipenem against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative pathogens by inhibiting class A and class C β-lactamases, particularly KPC. With the increasing prevalence of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) in China, evaluation of the in vitro activity of IMR is warranted. As part of the SMART surveillance program, Enterobacterales isolates were collected from 18 tertiary hospitals in China (2020-2022), including specimens from bloodstream, intra-abdominal, respiratory, and urinary tract infections (UTIs) in intensive care units (ICUs) and general wards. Species were identified by MALDI-TOF MS, and susceptibility was determined by broth microdilution. A total of 6182 Enterobacterales isolates were included, of which 19.1% were carbapenem-resistant. Higher rates of carbapenem resistance were observed among isolates from ICU patients and those causing urinary tract infections. IMR demonstrated substantially greater in vitro activity against CRKP than imipenem alone, resulting in a marked shift toward lower MIC distributions and an approximately fivefold reduction in the proportion of resistant isolates across both ICU and non-ICU settings. Compared with other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, IMR showed a higher proportion of isolates with MICs ≤1 mg/L and fewer isolates with elevated MICs than ceftazidime/avibactam or meropenem/vaborbactam, particularly among CRKP isolates. IMR exhibits in vitro activity against CRKP, particularly among isolates from ICU patients and those causing bloodstream infections. Our study suggests that IMR represents an important therapeutic option for infections caused by resistant Gram-negative pathogens, particularly carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; however, further clinical data are needed to confirm efficacy.

title: Antimicrobial resistance and molecular characterization of extended-spectrum β-lactamase/AmpC β-lactamase-producing Proteus mirabilis isolates from companion dogs in South Korea (2018-2024)
abstract: To investigate antimicrobial resistance profiles and molecular characteristics of third-generation cephalosporin- and cephamycin-resistant Proteus mirabilis isolated from clinically ill dogs across South Korea from 2018 through 2024. Antimicrobial susceptibility of isolates was assessed by broth microdilution. Molecular characteristics were determined by polymerase chain reaction and multilocus sequence typing. In total, 667 P mirabilis were isolated from skin/ear, feces, and urine/reproductive systems of companion dogs. Among them, 27.3% of isolates exhibited a multidrug-resistant (MDR) phenotype. Molecular characterization of 38 extended-spectrum β-lactamase (5.7%)/AmpC β-lactamase-carrying strains revealed a high prevalence of β-lactamase cephamycinase-2 gene blaCMY-2 (65.8%) and β-lactamase cefotaximase gene blaCTX-M variants, including blaCTX-M-65, blaCTX-M-15, and blaCTX-M-90. Multilocus sequence typing identified 16 distinct sequence types (STs), with ST135 (39.5%) and ST212 (21.1%) emerging as the most prevalent lineages. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the first major cluster contains 31 isolates (81.6%) across 10 STs centered around ST135, whereas the second cluster comprises 7 isolates (18.4%) across 6 STs centered on ST292. Notably, the ST135-centered cluster was associated with robust MDR phenotypes. These findings indicate that companion dogs harboring MDR P mirabilis are among several potential reservoirs within the One Health context. Especially, clone ST135 may serve as a primary evolutionary axis and a high-risk endemic clone within the Korean canine population. Our study highlights the critical role of dominant lineages in dissemination of extended-spectrum β-lactamase/AmpC β-lactamase genes and emphasizes the urgent need for continuous One Health surveillance to monitor potential transmission of these clones between companion animals and humans.

title: Differential regulation of conjugative transfer and OMV-mediated ARG delivery by iprovalicarb and cycluron: Implications for pathway-specific risk assessment
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major driver of the rapid dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) among bacteria. Non-antibiotic compounds can promote plasmid-mediated conjugative transfer. In waterfowl farming, waterfowl frequently move among water, soil, and feces, which serve as reservoirs for pesticides and ARGs and thus potential hotspots for ARG spread. However, whether outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), an emerging ARG transmission pathway, are regulated by pesticides and respond in a manner consistent with conjugation is unclear. In this study, two pesticides detected in waterfowl farm environments, iprovalicarb and cycluron were selected to investigate their effects on conjugative transfer and OMV-mediated ARG dissemination. Both pesticides significantly promoted RP4 plasmid conjugation frequency at sub-inhibitory concentrations. This effect was associated with elevated bacterial reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased membrane permeability and fluidity, enhanced interbacterial contact, and altered energy metabolism. However, their effects on the OMV pathway diverged: iprovalicarb increased OMV production and vesicle size and was associated with more bla-positive colonies after OMV exposure, whereas cycluron inhibited OMV production. This decoupling suggests that pesticides can differentially regulate conjugative and OMV-mediated ARG transfer. However, the bla gene was not stably inherited in recipient bacteria. Overall, these findings highlight the need to evaluate these two pathways separately when assessing the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Analytical instability and aqueous degradation of carbapenem antibiotics: formation of β-lactam-retaining transformation products
authors: Martinez I Quer A et al.
abstract: Carbapenems are last-resort antibiotics used to treat severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria. Despite their clinical importance and documented consumption, they remain largely undetected in environmental monitoring studies. This study investigated whether the lack of detection of carbapenems in environmental studies reflects analytical limitations, rapid degradation, or both. Sensitive LC-MS/MS methods were developed for selected carbapenems and used to assess compound stability under analytical and environmentally relevant conditions. All investigated carbapenems exhibited limited stability, with degradation strongly accelerated by methanol. Under environmentally relevant conditions, parent compounds degraded rapidly in river water, biofilm-containing water, and UV-exposed water, with little difference between treatments. High-resolution LC-MS/MS analysis revealed formation of multiple transformation products (TPs) retaining an intact β-lactam ring. Meropenem generated four β-lactam-retaining TPs, and faropenem generated four, several of which remained detectable long after disappearance of the parent compounds. These findings help explain the lack of detection of carbapenems in environmental surveys and demonstrate that disappearance of parent compounds does not necessarily imply elimination of β-lactam-containing structures. The persistence of β-lactam-retaining TPs suggests that environmental exposure and associated selective pressure may persist after parent carbapenems have degraded, highlighting the need for further investigation of their biological activity and potential role in antimicrobial resistance.

title: Bioinformatics for Healthcare Quality Management: Clinical Outcomes, Implementation Barriers, and Care Improvement
abstract: The bioinformatics-enabled workflows as quality-management tools have become central to modern healthcare, enabling genomic sequencing, transcriptomics, proteomics, and multiomics integration to support clinical decision-making. Despite expanding adoption, synthesized evidence on measurable clinical value and organizational, workforce, interoperability, governance, and equity barriers remains limited. To synthesize evidence on the contribution of bioinformatics-enabled workflows to healthcare quality improvement, care-process performance, clinical decision-making, patient outcomes, and implementation challenges from 2015 to 2025. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore. We included studies from real-world healthcare or public health settings where bioinformatics supported diagnostic quality, timeliness, treatment appropriateness, patient safety, and workflow efficiency, or operational decision-making, reporting quantitative outcomes including diagnostic yield, time-to-diagnosis, treatment modification, or economic impact. Twenty studies met the selection criteria, spanning precision oncology, pharmacogenomics, infectious disease surveillance, clinical genomics and rare disease diagnosis, and multiomics biomarker translation. Across these domains, bioinformatics-enabled workflows improved diagnostic yield (25%-40% in rare disease genomics) and diagnostic accuracy, and shortened time-to-diagnosis, from 4-6 weeks to as little as 3 days in acute pediatric care and from weeks to under 24 hours for pathogen genomic surveillance. Workflows also supported treatment modification, with matched or altered therapy in 33%-37% of oncology cases, and improved pathogen detection and antimicrobial-resistance monitoring. Economic evidence, although still limited, was favorable: first-line exome sequencing was cost-saving, with average reductions of approximately US$9000 per patient in rare disease diagnosis. Although precision medicine relies heavily on bioinformatics, improvements to infrastructure, consistent governance, and capacity building for clinical staff are essential to ensure its scalable and equitable implementation.

title: Phage-encoded PciP differentially regulates Pseudomonas aeruginosa swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms
abstract: is an opportunistic pathogen whose intrinsic antibiotic resistance and complex virulence regulatory networks pose major clinical challenges. Bacteriophages and their encoded proteins have emerged as potential modulators of bacterial physiology, yet the mechanisms by which phage proteins influence bacterial virulence remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified PciP, an early protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, which suppresses pyocyanin production and swarming motility in. PciP reduces PQS levels and suppresses quorum-sensing gene transcription. PciP associates with CheV, and genetic analysis indicates that CheV is required for the PciP-mediated inhibition of swarming but not for the PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production. Expression of PciP attenuates virulence in infection models. Together, these findings reveal that PciP differentially modulates swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms. These results provide mechanistic insights into how a phage-encoded protein reprograms host regulatory networks.IMPORTANCEis a major opportunistic pathogen that is increasingly difficult to treat due to intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance. Bacteriophages encode diverse proteins that can interfere with bacterial regulatory networks, yet many remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we characterize PciP, a protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, and show that it modulates bacterial motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes through distinct mechanisms. PciP associates with CheV and inhibits swarming motility in a CheV-dependent manner, whereas PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production persists in the absence of CheV. These combined effects significantly reduce pathogenicity in both animal and plant infection models. This study advances our understanding of phage-host interactions by demonstrating that a phage-encoded protein can differentially modulate host regulatory outputs via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms.

title: Impact of ESKAPE pathogens on the One Health framework considering epidemiology and environmental occurrence
abstract: SUMMARYThe ESKAPE group of pathogens represents one of the most critical threats to global health due to their capacity to evade antimicrobial treatments. This review provides a structured synthesis of the literature addressing antimicrobial resistance mechanisms, epidemiological relevance, clinical impact, and emerging strategies for containment within a One Health framework. Relevant studies and surveillance reports were analyzed to characterize the global distribution and burden of these organisms across human, animal, and environmental settings. The evidence indicates that ESKAPE pathogens remain leading causes of healthcare-associated infections while increasingly being identified in non-clinical reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance. Recent findings point to sustained high morbidity and mortality associated with these pathogens, driven by the expansion of multidrug-resistant lineages, and the limited effectiveness of current therapeutic options. Key challenges identified include gaps in surveillance integration, the spread of resistance determinants across sectors, and variability in infection control practices. Addressing these issues requires coordinated strategies that integrate surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and the development of novel therapeutics within a comprehensive One Health approach.

title: Comparative analysis of various infection models to provide methodological insights for the characterization of new antivirulence drugs to fight antibioresistance
abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health burden, amplified by the rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Among priority pathogens, the ESKAPEE group represents a critical threat due to their high prevalence in healthcare-associated infections, and their capacity to acquire multidrug resistance. Antivirulence strategies, aiming at disarming pathogens rather than inhibiting their growth, constitute a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. Their development, however, is hindered by the lack of suitable experimental models to evaluate virulence and antivirulence efficacy. Here, we establish complementaryandinfection models to characterize pathogenicity and assess antivirulence activity against clinically relevant ESKAPEE bacteria (). We developed a robust nitric oxide (NO)-basedassay that mimics host immune nitrosative stress and enables quantitative evaluation of bacterial resistance to innate immune defenses. In parallel, we established comparative insect infection models usingandspecies, allowing reproducible assessment of bacterial virulence across multiple hosts and pathogens. These models highlighted marked differences in pathogenic potential depending on both bacterial species and host background. As a proof of concept, we applied these systems to characterize NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting the DNA repair protein Mfd. NM102 significantly reduced bacterial survival under NO stressand decreased bacterial burdenin insect infection models. Together, our results demonstrate that combining immune-mimickingassays with complementary insect models provides a powerful and ethically acceptable platform to study bacterial pathogenicity and to accelerate the development of innovative antivirulence therapeutics to combat AMR.IMPORTANCEBacterial infections remain a major public health challenge, worsened by the rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance. Among the most concerning pathogens are the ESKAPEE bacteria, which frequently cause hospital-acquired infections and are often resistant to multiple antibiotics. Antivirulence strategies offer promising alternatives to traditional treatments by disarming bacteria rather than killing them, potentially reducing the risk of resistance. However, progress in this field has been limited by the lack of reliable models to measure bacterial virulence and evaluate antivirulence compounds. In this study, we developed complementary models to better assess bacterial pathogenicity and treatment efficacy. We created anassay that mimics immune defenses and established insect infection models to compare virulence across pathogens and hosts. Using these systems, we tested NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting bacterial DNA repair. NM102 reduced bacterial survival and infection severity, highlighting the potential of antivirulence approaches as innovative therapies against drug-resistant infections.

title: The global landscape of Campylobacter: genomic epidemiology, AMR trends, and the path to vaccine development
abstract: species, particularlyand, are leading causes of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide, responsible for an estimated 500 million cases of acute diarrheal illness annually. Despite their global prevalence and association with severe post-infectious sequelae such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, no licensed vaccine exists, and the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance further complicates clinical management. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the epidemiology, genomic diversity, antimicrobial resistance mechanisms, and vaccine development strategies forspecies, with emphasis on global trends and public health relevance in the United States. Through a One Health lens, we examine transmission across human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, and highlight the role of integrated genomic surveillance in tracking clonal expansion, horizontal gene transfer, and resistance dissemination. We also examine historical and current approaches to vaccine development, including whole-cell, subunit, glycoconjugate, and genomics-guided antigen discovery strategies. Challenges such as antigenic variability, phase variation, and inadequate experimental models have impeded progress, though recent genomics-informed interventions show promise in both poultry and human contexts. Continued investment in genomic surveillance, antimicrobial resistance, and rational antigen selection will be essential for developing effective vaccines and reducing the global burden of campylobacteriosis.

title: A putative GtrB-like glycosyltransferase modulates cation-dependent BCP8-2 phage infection and cell surface structure in Bacillus cereus
abstract: is a foodborne pathogen of growing concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial resistance. To identify host determinants influencing susceptibility to phage BCP8-2, a mini-Tntransposon mutant library ofATCC 14579 was constructed and screened for altered phage susceptibility. A mutant (BC2012) showing partial resistance carried an insertion in(previously), encoding a putative GtrB-like bactoprenol glycosyltransferase.
